nodes.name: Set $aRb$
nodes.statement: For $a, b \in R$, denote by $aRb$ the set $\{arb| r \in R\}$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
nodes.label: def:aRb

nodes.name: Left/Right Ideal
nodes.statement: A \textit{left/right ideal} $I$ of a ring $R$ is an additive subgroup of $R$ such that $rI \subseteq I$ for all $r \in R$ or $Ir \subseteq I$ for all $r \in R$, respectively.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
nodes.label: def:left_right_ideal

nodes.name: Two-sided Ideal
nodes.statement: A two-sided ideal is a subset of $R$ that is both left and right ideal of $R$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
nodes.label: def:two_sided_ideal

nodes.name: Product of Ideals
nodes.statement: A product of (left/right/two-sided) ideals $I$ and $J$ is the ideal $IJ$ generated by the set of all pairwise products of elements of $I$ and $J$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
nodes.label: def:product_of_ideals

nodes.name: Prime Ring
nodes.statement: A ring is prime if we have $I = 0$ or $J = 0$ whenever $IJ = 0$ for some left ideals $I$ and $J$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
nodes.label: def:is_prime_ring

nodes.statement: A ring is prime if and only if for all $a, b \in R, aRb = 0$ implies $a = 0$ or $b = 0$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
nodes.label: thm:prime_ring_equiv

nodes.statement: $(\Rightarrow)$ Suppose $aRb = 0$. Then $(Ra)(Rb) = 0$, thus by primality $Ra = 0$ or $Rb = 0$. In the former case we get $a = 1 \cdot a \in Ra$ and thus $a = 0$ and in the latter case we get $b = 1 \cdot b \in Rb$ and thus $b = 0$. $(\Leftarrow)$ Suppose $IJ = 0$. Then $aRb \subseteq IJ = 0$ for any $a \in I$ and $b \in J$. By assumption we get $a = 0$ or $b = 0$, so at least one of $I$ and $J$ is zero.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.statement: A ring is prime if and only if for all two-sided ideals $I$ and $J$, $IJ = 0$ implies $I = 0$ or $J = 0$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
nodes.label: thm:prime_ring_equiv'

nodes.statement: $(\Rightarrow)$ Two-sided ideals are left ideals, so the result follows directly from definiton. $(\Leftarrow)$ Suppose $aRb = 0$. Then $(RaR)(RbR) = 0$. By assumption $RaR = 0$ or $RbR = 0$. Thus $a = 0$ or $b = 0$ so the result follows from the previous theorem.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Simple Ring
nodes.statement: A ring is simple if it has no nontrivial two-sided ideals.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
nodes.label: def:IsSimpleRing

nodes.statement: A simple ring is prime.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
nodes.label: thm:simple_ring_is_prime

nodes.statement: Suppose $IJ = 0$. If both $I$ and $J$ are nonzero, they must be equal to $R$ by simplicity. But $RR = R \neq 0$, a contradiction.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Orthogonal Elements
nodes.statement: Two elements $a, b \in R$ are orthogonal if $ab = ba = 0$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
nodes.label: def:IsOrthogonal

nodes.statement: If $e, f \in R$ are orthogonal idempotents and $f \neq 0$, then the left ideal generated by $1 - e - f$ is strictly smaller than the left ideal generated by $1 - e$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings
nodes.label: thm:one_sub_e_larger_span_on_sub_e_sub_f

nodes.statement: Note that $(1 - e - f)(1 - e) = 1 - e - f$, and hence $x(1 - e - f) = x(1 - e - f)(1 - e) \in R(1 - e)$ for every $x \in R$. This proves that $R(1 - e) \supseteq R(1 - e - f)$. We have $f = f(1 - e) \in R(1 - e)$, while $f = x(1 - e - f)$ with $x \in R$ implies $0 = f(1 - f) = x(1 - e - f)(1 - f) = x(1 - e - f) = f$, a contradiction. Therefore, $R(1 - e) \neq R(1 - e - f)$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.name: Corner Ring Set
nodes.statement: The set of the corner ring is $eRe$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings
nodes.label: def:corner_ring

nodes.statement: An element $x$ is in the set $e R f$ if and only if $x = e x f$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings
nodes.label: thm:characterization_of_corner_elements

nodes.statement: $(\Rightarrow)$ Suppose $x \in e R f$. Then $x = e y f$ for some $y \in R$. But then $e x f = e e y f f = e y f = x$. $(\Leftarrow)$ Clear.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.statement: An element $x$ of $R$ is in the corner ring if and only if $x = e x e$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings
nodes.label: thm:characterization_of_corner_ring_elements

nodes.statement: Application of theorem \ref{thm:characterization_of_corner_elements}.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.statement: An element $x$ of the corner ring is of the form $e y e$ for some $y \in R$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings
nodes.label: thm:characterization_of_corner_ring_elements'

nodes.statement: Clear from the theorem \ref{thm:characterization_of_corner_ring_elements}
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.statement: The corner ring is a (non-unital) subring of $R$. It has its own unit $e$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings
nodes.label: thm:corner_ring_is_ring

nodes.statement: If $a, b \in eRe$, then $a + b = e a e + e b e = e (a + b) e$ so $eRe$ is closed under addition. If $a, b \in eRe$, then $a b = e a e e b e = e a b e$, so $eRe$ is closed under multiplication. Distributivity and associativity are inherited from $R$. Since $e a = eeae = eae = a = eae = eaee = ae$ for any $a \in eRe$, $e$ is the unit of $eRe$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.statement: If $R$ is left artinian, then the corner ring is left artinian.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings
nodes.label: thm:corner_ring_artinian

nodes.statement: Let $L_1 \supseteq L_2 \supseteq \ldots$ be a descending chain of left ideals in $eRe$. Then $ RL_1 \supseteq RL_2 \supseteq \ldots$ is a descending chain of left ideals in $R$. Since $R$ is left artinian, this chain stabilizes. But then so does $eRL_1 \supseteq eRL_2 \supseteq \ldots$. But since $eRL_i = eReL_i = L_i$, the chain $L_1 \supseteq L_2 \supseteq \ldots$ also stabilizes.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.statement: If $R$ is a prime ring, then the corner ring is prime.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings
nodes.label: thm:corner_ring_prime

nodes.statement: Suppose $aeReb = 0$ for $a, b \in eRe$. Then $ae = a = 0$ or $eb = b = 0$ by \ref{thm:prime_ring_equiv}, and by the same theorem, the ring is prime.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.statement: If all elements in a ring are left invertible, then the ring is a division ring.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings
nodes.label: thm:all_left_inv_div_ring

nodes.statement: Let $x \in R$ be arbitrary. Then $yx = 1$ for some $y \in R$. Since $y$ is left invertible, there exists some $z$ such that $zy = 1$. By uniqueness of left and right inverses of $y$ it must hold that $z = x$. Thus $x$ is invertible.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.name: Brauer's lemma
nodes.statement: Suppose $L$ is a minimal (left) ideal of $R$ and $L^2 \neq 0$. Then there exists an idempotent $e \in L$ such that $L = Re$ and $eRe$ is a division ring.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings
nodes.label: thm:brauer_lemma

nodes.statement:
By assumption, there exists $y \in L$ such that $Ly 
eq 0$. By minimality $L = Ly$. Thus, there exists $e \in L$ such that $e y = y$. Let $J \subseteq L$ be the set of elements in $L$ that annihilate $y$ from the left. The element $e$ is not in $J$, therefore $J = 0$ by minimality of $L$. Rearranging the previous equality, $(e^2 - e) y = 0$ which implies $e^2 = e$, since $e^2 - e$ is in $J = 0$. Clearly $e 
eq 0$, and so by minimality $Re = L$. Let $a \in eRe$ be non-zero. Then $0 
eq Ra = Reae \leq Re = L$, so $Ra = L$. Thus $e \in Ra$, so $e = r a$ for some $r \in R$. Then $e = e^2 = e r e a$, so $a$ is invertible in $eRe$. We are done by ef{thm:all_left_inv_div_ring}

nodes.statement: $J$ is a left ideal of $R$ contained in $L$.

nodes.statement: Let $a, b \in J$. Then $(a + b) y = a y + b y = 0$, so $(a + b) \in J$. For any $x \in R$, $x a y = 0$ so $xa \in J$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.statement: (Already proven in Mathlib) A nonzero left artinian ring has a minimal left ideal.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings
nodes.label: thm:artinian_has_minimal_left_ideal

nodes.statement: If minimal left ideal does not exist, then starting with any nonzero left ideal, we can allways find a strictly smaller nonzero left ideal. We can thus construct an infinite strictly decreasing sequence of left ideals, which contradicts the left artinian property.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.name: Set of Matrix Units
nodes.statement: A set $e_{ij}$ for $i, j \in [1, n]$ is a \textit{set of matrix units} of $R$ if $$ e_{ij}e_{kl} = \begin{cases} e_{il} & \mid j = k \\ 0 & \mid \text{otherwise}\end{cases} $$ and $\sum_{i=1}^n e_{ii} = 1$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings
nodes.label: def:matrixunits

nodes.statement: If $R$ has a set of matrix units $e_{ij}$, then $R$ is isomorphic to the ring of $n \times n$ matrices over the corner ring $e_{11}Re_{11}$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings
nodes.label: thm:ring_with_matrix_units

nodes.statement: For $a \in R$, denote $a_{ij} = e_{1i}ae_{j1}$. Then $e_{11}a_{ij}e_{11} = e_{11}e_{1i}ae_{j1}e_{11} = e_{1i}ae_{j1}$ by the property of matrix units. Then, the map $\phi$ claimed to be the isomorphism is $a \mapsto (a_{ij})_{i,j=1}^n$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.statement: $\phi$ is additive.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings
3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.statement: The map is multiplicative.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.statement: The $(i,j)$ entry of $\phi(a)\phi(b)$ is equal to $$ \sum_{k=1}^n e_{1i}ae_{k1}e_{1k}be_{j1} = e_{1i}a \sum_{k=1}^n e_{kk} be_{j1} = e_{1i}abe_{j1}, $$ which is the $(i,j)$ entry of $\phi(ab)$. Therefore, $\phi(ab) = \phi(a)\phi(b)$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.statement: The map is injective.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.statement: Suppose $a_{ij} = 0$ for all $i, j$. Then $e_{ii}ae_{jj} = e_{1i}a_{ij}e_{j1} = 0$. Therefore, $a = a(\sum_{i=1}^n e_{ii}) = \sum_{i=1}^n ae_{ii} = \sum_{i,j=1}^n e_{ii}ae_{jj} = 0$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.statement: The map is surjective.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.statement: Note the $\phi(e_{k1}ae_{1l})_{kl} = e_{1k}e_{k1}a e_{1l}e_{l1} = e_{11}ae_{11}$ and $\phi(e_{k1}ae_{1l})_{ab} = e_{1a}e_{k1}a e_{1l}e_{b1} = 0$ if $a \neq k$ or $b \neq l$, so $\phi(e_{k1}ae_{1l})$ is a matrix whose all entries are zero, except the $k$-th and $l$-th entry is non-zero, and can take arbitrary value in $e_{11}ae_{11}$. By additivity, the map is surjective.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.statement: If a ring $R$ has a set of pairwise orthogonal idempotents $e_{ii}$ and \begin{itemize} \item $e_{1i} \in e_{11}Re_{ii}$ for all $i$, \item $e_{e1} \in e_{ii}Re_{11}$ for all $i$, \item $e_{1i}e_{e1} = e_{11}$ \item $e_{i1}e_{1i} = e_{ii}$ for all $i$, \end{itemize} then $R$ has matrix units.

nodes.label: thm:criterion_for_matrix_units

nodes.statement: Let $e, f \in R$ be nonzero orthogonal idempotents and $R$ a prime ring. Also let $eRe$ and $fRf$ be division rings. Then there exist $u, v \in R$ such that $u \in eRf$ and $v \in fRe$ such that $uv = e$ and $vu = f$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings
nodes.label: thm:orthogonal_idempotents_division_ring

nodes.statement: Since $eRe$ is a division ring, there exists $c \in R$ such that $(eafbe)(ece) = e$. Let $u = eaf$ and $v = fbece$, which belong to $eRf$ and $fRe$ respectively. Then $uv = eafbece = e$. Note that $vu \in fRf$ and that $vuv = ve = v = fv$. Therefore, $(vu - f) v = 0$

Suppose $eafRe = 0$. Then $e = 0$ by theorem \ref{thm:prime_ring_equiv'}, a contradiction. Therefore, there exists $b$ such that $eafbe \neq 0$.

nodes.statement: If a prime ring $R$ contains pairwise orthogonal idempotents $e_{ii}$ with sum $1$ and $e_{ii}Re_{ii}$ is a division ring for every $i$, then $R$ is isomorphic to $M_n(e_{11}Re_{11})$.

By theorem \ref{thm:criterion_for_matrix_units}, $R$ has matrix units, and by theorem \ref{thm:ring_with_matrix_units} it is isomorphic to $M_n(e_{11}Re_{11})$.

nodes.statement: $f = f(1 - e) + fe = f + fe$. Thus $fe = 0$. Similarly, $ef = 0$. Therefore, $f$ and $e$ are orthogonal. Note that $x \in fRf \iff \exists r, x = f r f = f \iff \exists r, x = f(1 - e) r (1 - e) f \iff x \in f(1 - e) R (1 - e) f$.

nodes.name: Artin Wedderburn for prime rings
nodes.statement: If $R$ is a prime ring and artinian, then $R$ is isomorphic to $M_n(D)$ for some division ring $D$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings
nodes.label: thm:artin_wedderburn_for_prime

nodes.statement: Since $R$ is artinian, it contains a minimal nonzero left ideal $L$. If $L^2 = 0$, this would imply by the prime condition that $L = 0$, a contradiction. Therefore, $L^2 \neq 0$. By the Brauer lemma, there exists an idempotent $e \in L$ such that $L = Re_{11}$ and $e_{11}Re_{11}$ is a division ring. By theorem \ref{thm:one_sub_e_larger_span_on_sub_e_sub_f} for $e = 0$ and $f = e_{11}$ we have that $R \supsetneq R(1 - e_{11})$. Suppose $e_{11} \neq 1$. Then $(1 - e_{11}) R (1 - e_{11})$ is a nonzero ring. It is also prime and artinian by theorems \ref{thm:corner_ring_prime} and \ref{thm:corner_ring_artinian}. Repeating the argument for this ring, we obtain $e_{22}$ such that $e_{22}(1 - e_{11}) R (1 - e_{11})e_{22}$ is a division ring. Since $e_{22} \in (1 - e_{11}) R (1 - e_{11})$ then must be orthogonal, as by the theorem \ref{thm:idempotents_orthogonal}. Further $R (1 - e_{11}) \supsetneq R (1 - e_{11} - e_{22})$. Repeating this process, we get a sequence of $e_{ii}$ and a sequence of left ideals $R(1 - e_{11} - \ldots - e_{ii})$. By the artinian condition, this sequence must stabilize, so for some $n$, meaning that $\sum_{i = 1}^{n} e_{ii} = 1$. $e_{ii}$ are pairwise orthogonal and are idempotent. Additionally, all $e_{ii} R e_{ii}$ are division rings. By theorem \ref{thm:orthogonal_idempotents_division_ring_matrix}, $R$ is isomorphic to $M_n(e_{11}Re_{11})$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.name: Artin Wedderburn for simple rings
nodes.statement: If $R$ is a simple ring, then $R$ is isomorphic to $M_n(D)$ for some division ring $D$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings
nodes.label: thm:artin_wedderburn_for_simple

nodes.statement: Since $R$ is simple, it is prime. By theorem \ref{thm:artin_wedderburn_for_prime}, $R$ is isomorphic to $M_n(D)$ for some division ring $D$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Artin-Wedderburn Theorem for prime and simple rings

nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a semisimple ring. Then, $R$ is isomorphic to a direct product of simple, artinian rings.
nodes.section: 4 Generalization to semisimple ring
nodes.label: thm:semisimple_direct_product_simple_artinian

nodes.statement: WLOG, suppose, $R$ is not simple. We know that $R$ is (left) artinian, which is a stronger condition that being (two-sided) artinian. Since it is (two-sided) artinian, it must contain a nontrivial minimal (two-sided) ideal $I$, which is therefore simple. Since $R$ is semisimple, $I$ must be a direct summand of $R$ (AS A LEFT $R$-module). Thus, $R = I \oplus J$ for some (left) ideal $J$. Then $1 = i + j$ for some $i \in I$ and $j \in J$ . Note that $I$ and $J$ are both nontrivial. Thus, we can repeat the process of splitting $J$ (if it is not simple) into a direct product of simple, artinian rings. Since $R$ is artinian, this process must stabilize, and we get a direct product of simple, artinian rings. Apply the \ref{thm:artin_wedderburn_for_simple} to each of the simple, artinian rings to get the desired result.
nodes.section: 4 Generalization to semisimple ring

nodes.statement: We know that it is a left ideal. For arbitrary $x \in R$, write $x = x i + x j$. Let $y \in J$ be arbitrary. Then $y x = y x i + y x j = 0 + y x j \in J$, where $y x i = 0$ since it is in $J I$. Thus $J$ is also a right ideal.

nodes.statement: Let $x = x_i + x_j$ where $x_i = x i \in I$ and $x j \in J$. Similarly, let $y = y_i + y_j$. Then $x y = x_i y_i + x_i y_j + x_j y_i + x_j y_j = x_i y_i + x_j y_j$ since $x_i y_j = 0$ and $x_j y_i = 0$ by the previous claims. Thus, the map $x \mapsto (x_i, x_j)$ is a ring homomorphism. Injective: Suppose $x i = x_j = 0$. Then $x = x 1 = x (i + j) = 0$. Surjective: let $(x_i, x_j)\in I \times J$ be arbitrary. Let $x = x_i + x_j$. Note that $x_i = x_i i + x_i j = x_i i$ by orthogonality of $I$ and $J$. Similarly $x_j = x_j j$. Then $x i = (x_i + x_j) i = x_i i = x_i$ and similarly $x j = x_j$. Thus $(x_i, x_j)$ is the image of $x$.

nodes.statement: Let $K \subseteq I$ be a left $I$-submodule of $I$, where $I$ is treated as a unital ring. Then $K$ is a left submodule of $R$.
nodes.section: 4 Generalization to semisimple ring

nodes.statement: Let $r \in R$ and $k \in K$. Then $r k = r 1 k = r (i + j) k = r i k + r j k = r i k \in K$ since $k \in K$, $r i \in I$ and $r j k = 0$ as $j \in J$ and $k \in I$ and we know $J I = 0$. Thus $K$ is closed under left multiplication by element of $R$.
nodes.section: 4 Generalization to semisimple ring

nodes.statement: Both $I$ and $J$ are artinian (as rings).
nodes.section: 4 Generalization to semisimple ring

nodes.statement: They are both submodules of $R$ which is assumed to be artinian. Submodules of artinian modules are artinian. Note that $R$ is artinian since it is semisimple. Thus they are artinian as left $R$-modules. Let $K_1 \supseteq K_2 \supseteq \ldots$ be a descending chain of left ideals (modules) in ring $I$. By the previous claim, they are also left ideals in $R$. Since $R$ is artinian, this chain stabilizes. But then so does $K_1 \supseteq K_2 \supseteq \ldots$. Thus $I$ is artinian. Same argument applies to $J$.
nodes.section: 4 Generalization to semisimple ring

nodes.statement: $J$ is (left) semisimple.
nodes.section: 4 Generalization to semisimple ring

nodes.statement: A submodule of a semisimple module is semisimple. Thus $J$ is semisimple as a left $R$-module. Let $K \subseteq J$ be a left $J$-submodule. Then $K$ is a left $R$-submodule by the previous claim. Since $R$ is semisimple, every submodules of a submodules has a direct complement, call it $K'$. Then $J = K \oplus K'$, as $R$-modules. Since $K'$ is a left $R$-submodule, it is also a left $J$-submodule. Thus $J$ is semisimple as a left $J$-module.
